title: The $25,000 Slate truck is proudly bare-bones. I think these add-ons are worth the extra money.
summary: The base model Slate has a lot of driving verve — but here's what I couldn't live without. Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Slate's main pitch is affordability. Its no-frills base model is just under $25,000 before charges. It's second core tenet: personalization. You can add hundreds of configurable options. I drove the truck on Tuesday. Here's what I'd add to mine. The Slate truck doesn't have a typical key. Unlike today's cars — which pack proximity sensors inside a little plastic box that runs tech that allows drivers to start the engine via a push-start button — the Slate has a simple solution. Drivers put a square key into a square slot. The instrument display flicks on. A single bell chimes. That's it. There is no theatrical lighting sequence, symphony-like entrance music, or enormous touchscreen springing to life. Even the windows are simpler. They're controlled by manual hand cranks. In my test, it took six or seven spins before the glass disappeared into the door panel. The deliberately plain interior captures Slate's entire pitch: Modern cars are too complicated , too expensive, and too eager to make every grocery trip feel like a Silicon Valley hype cycle. Slate's $24,950 electric truck (a little over $26,000, after delivery fees) starts with the basics. Buyers can then use the company's accessory marketplace to add back the features they care about, including speakers, upgraded upholstery, colorful body wraps, storage accessories, and towing equipment. It is a very different way to make money after selling a car. While other automakers increasingly rely on software subscriptions and features delivered through updates, Slate wants customers to buy physical upgrades. I drove a prototype on Tuesday and came away pleasantly surprised. The inexpensive truck was roomy, balanced, and genuinely fun to drive. But the experience also showed me which modern conveniences I would miss. These are the add-ons I'd buy to make the bare-bones Slate truck livable — plus the options I'd choose if money were no object. My non-negotiables I found five options on Slate's marketplace that I couldn't live without. That bumped the car's price well into the $30,000 range. Slate I found five add-ons on Slate's marketplace that I'd need. More seats The base Slate is a two-seat pickup, which could be perfect for a small business hauling products around town. It would be considerably less useful for my life, unless I suddenly decided to stop driving my friends anywhere. So my first upgrade would be Slate's squareback SUV kit. It adds a second-row bench, increases capacity from two people to five, and raises the price from $24,950 to $29,950. Speakers My friends would be mad if that car were silent. I spend too much time in cars listening to podcasts and Beyoncé to rely on the natural symphonies of the roadway, so I would add Slate's $250 integrated speaker system. Buyers committed to the stripped-down lifestyle can instead choose a universal speaker mount, though Slate has not yet announced its price. Extra locks I would also spend $100 on a locking tailgate. Leaving the contents of the bed available to anyone walking past feels a little too bare-bones, even for Slate. Accessories for a bike rack Finally, I bike enough that I would need a rear-mounted carrier and a tow hitch to hold it. Together, those add another $700. That brings my supposedly bare-bones Slate to about $31,000 before taxes and destination fees. At that price, it starts bumping into vehicles like the base Ford Maverick and Nissan Leaf — both of which arrive with power windows, infotainment screens, and fewer decisions to make before leaving the dealership. If money didn't hold me back… My dream build would push nearly $35,000. Slate OK, but what if I decided to splash out? My dream Slate would include a bevy of wildly unnecessary (but fun!) upgrades. I would start with a blue body wrap, a white roof, matching wheel covers, and yellow accents. Who needs that $1,056 anyway? Naturally, the yellow would continue inside. And because I would also want to project outdoorsy ruggedness, I would add a rear-mounted spare tire, an upgraded bumper, fender flares, running boards, and a roof rack that I absolutely do not know how to use. That adds another $2,374.94. By the time I finished, my dream Slate had 28 accessories, including five that Slate has not priced yet. The running total reached $34,949 before those final bits and bobs. That excess is part of Slate's appeal. Automakers have spent years filling parking lots with crossover SUVs that increasingly blur together. It can be difficult to distinguish a Toyota RAV4 from a Honda CR-V or Mazda CX-5 waiting in the school pickup line. The era of the affordable personality car — think the Volkswagen Beetle or Chrysler PT Cruiser — has largely faded. Slate gives buyers an unusual amount of freedom to make the truck look like their own, right down to a new partnership with Crayola . Whether that is enough to create a mass-market hit remains to be seen. But after years of increasingly interchangeable cars, it is at least fun to build one with a little imagination. summary_html:
The base model Slate has a lot of driving verve — but here's what I couldn't live without.

Ben Shimkus/Business Insider

  • Slate's main pitch is affordability. Its no-frills base model is just under $25,000 before charges.
  • It's second core tenet: personalization. You can add hundreds of configurable options.
  • I drove the truck on Tuesday. Here's what I'd add to mine.

The Slate truck doesn't have a typical key.

Unlike today's cars — which pack proximity sensors inside a little plastic box that runs tech that allows drivers to start the engine via a push-start button — the Slate has a simple solution.

Drivers put a square key into a square slot. The instrument display flicks on. A single bell chimes.

That's it. There is no theatrical lighting sequence, symphony-like entrance music, or enormous touchscreen springing to life.

Even the windows are simpler. They're controlled by manual hand cranks. In my test, it took six or seven spins before the glass disappeared into the door panel.

The deliberately plain interior captures Slate's entire pitch: Modern cars are too complicated, too expensive, and too eager to make every grocery trip feel like a Silicon Valley hype cycle.

Slate's $24,950 electric truck (a little over $26,000, after delivery fees) starts with the basics. Buyers can then use the company's accessory marketplace to add back the features they care about, including speakers, upgraded upholstery, colorful body wraps, storage accessories, and towing equipment.

It is a very different way to make money after selling a car. While other automakers increasingly rely on software subscriptions and features delivered through updates, Slate wants customers to buy physical upgrades.

I drove a prototype on Tuesday and came away pleasantly surprised. The inexpensive truck was roomy, balanced, and genuinely fun to drive.

But the experience also showed me which modern conveniences I would miss.

These are the add-ons I'd buy to make the bare-bones Slate truck livable — plus the options I'd choose if money were no object.

My non-negotiablesI found five options on Slate's marketplace that I couldn't live without. That bumped the car's price well into the $30,000 range.

Slate

I found five add-ons on Slate's marketplace that I'd need.

More seats

The base Slate is a two-seat pickup, which could be perfect for a small business hauling products around town. It would be considerably less useful for my life, unless I suddenly decided to stop driving my friends anywhere.

So my first upgrade would be Slate's squareback SUV kit. It adds a second-row bench, increases capacity from two people to five, and raises the price from $24,950 to $29,950.

Speakers

My friends would be mad if that car were silent.

I spend too much time in cars listening to podcasts and Beyoncé to rely on the natural symphonies of the roadway, so I would add Slate's $250 integrated speaker system. Buyers committed to the stripped-down lifestyle can instead choose a universal speaker mount, though Slate has not yet announced its price.

Extra locks

I would also spend $100 on a locking tailgate. Leaving the contents of the bed available to anyone walking past feels a little too bare-bones, even for Slate.

Accessories for a bike rack

Finally, I bike enough that I would need a rear-mounted carrier and a tow hitch to hold it. Together, those add another $700.

That brings my supposedly bare-bones Slate to about $31,000 before taxes and destination fees.

At that price, it starts bumping into vehicles like the base Ford Maverick and Nissan Leaf — both of which arrive with power windows, infotainment screens, and fewer decisions to make before leaving the dealership.

If money didn't hold me back…My dream build would push nearly $35,000.

Slate

OK, but what if I decided to splash out?

My dream Slate would include a bevy of wildly unnecessary (but fun!) upgrades.

I would start with a blue body wrap, a white roof, matching wheel covers, and yellow accents. Who needs that $1,056 anyway?

Naturally, the yellow would continue inside. And because I would also want to project outdoorsy ruggedness, I would add a rear-mounted spare tire, an upgraded bumper, fender flares, running boards, and a roof rack that I absolutely do not know how to use.

That adds another $2,374.94.

By the time I finished, my dream Slate had 28 accessories, including five that Slate has not priced yet. The running total reached $34,949 before those final bits and bobs.

That excess is part of Slate's appeal.

Automakers have spent years filling parking lots with crossover SUVs that increasingly blur together. It can be difficult to distinguish a Toyota RAV4 from a Honda CR-V or Mazda CX-5 waiting in the school pickup line.

The era of the affordable personality car — think the Volkswagen Beetle or Chrysler PT Cruiser — has largely faded.

Slate gives buyers an unusual amount of freedom to make the truck look like their own, right down to a new partnership with Crayola.

Whether that is enough to create a mass-market hit remains to be seen. But after years of increasingly interchangeable cars, it is at least fun to build one with a little imagination.

title: Building ReproSpec: Portable Evidence Bundles and Offline Replay for Node.js
summary:
The Maintainer Problem Open-source maintainers face a dual crisis: a high volume of incomplete or platform-dependent bug reports ("works on my machine"), and a growing security risk when triaging pull requests that require running untrusted test suites locally. When a bug report is filed, maintainers often must choose between setting up a matching VM environment or triaging based on static text logs. The Information Gap in Ordinary Logs Ordinary logs are useful, but they usually do not include a standardized integrity manifest, a portable environment summary, and a documented local replay workflow in one bundle. ReproSpec is an experimental CLI and evidence-bundle format designed to bridge this gap. 1. Bundle Structure A ReproSpec bundle contains the following schema layout ( reprospec.bundle/v0.1-alpha ): manifest.json : Metadata, schema version, and security exceptions. command.json : Captured command parameters, exit code, and duration. environment.json : Node runtime details, scrubbed environment variables. stdout.txt / stderr.txt : Process logs. integrity.json : SHA-256 hash index of the declared files. EVIDENCE_CARD.md : A human-readable markdown report card. 2. Capture & Redaction Workflow When you run reprospec capture -- , ReproSpec: Spawns the command and records its output streams. Slices each of stdout and stderr streams individually to enforce a strict 10MB limit. Runs a regex redaction processor to remove supported credential patterns (such as ghp_ tokens) from stdout, stderr, environment keys, and command arguments. ⚠️ Argument Immutability : ReproSpec executes the captured command with its original arguments to ensure program behavior is unchanged. Redaction is applied only to the persisted evidence representation. 3. Integrity Limitations Verification re-calculates hashes against integrity.json . ⚠️ Important Limit : This only detects changes relative to the SHA-256 hashes recorded in the bundle manifest. A party able to rewrite the entire bundle could also recompute those hashes. It does not prove author identity or captured trace truthfulness. 4. Replay Sandbox Parity & Boundaries Immutable Source Snapshot : Capture stores the required source content inside the evidence bundle under snapshot/ , with relative paths, sizes, and SHA-256 hashes in snapshot.json and the bundle integrity manifest. Writable Disposable Execution : Before replay, ReproSpec verifies the immutable snapshot and copies it into a new ephemeral execution workspace. Only that disposable copy is mounted writable, so ordinary build and test commands can create dist , coverage, cache, and temporary files. No Original Checkout Mount : The original checkout and evidence bundle are not mounted into replay. allowWorkspaceMount is disabled and blocked in the Alpha.2 replay path. Output Handling : Replay records stdout, stderr, the exit-code oracle result, and files created, modified, or deleted in the execution workspace. The workspace and generated files are removed after success, failure, or timeout; generated files are never added back to the evidence snapshot. Dependency Isolation : An ephemeral build container uses npm ci with network access to fetch packages based on package-lock.json . It runs without host credentials, home-directory mounts, Docker socket access, or inherited variables. Offline Replay : The actual replay container runs offline with --network none . Host Check : The CLI compares git status before and after replay, failing if any host changes occur. 5. Lessons from the Three-Repository Pilot During early testing against real repositories, we encountered several portability limits: Vercel's ms package : Replay failed because Jest 30 preset resolution ( ts-jest ) failed to resolve correctly relative to the isolated workspace root under Node 20. dotenv package : The exact public commit c0e32b8267b69a438bc0cc31345f73b5e2f037db passed the Node.js 20 baseline and Alpha.2 clean-room replay. Its build and test workflow generated dist and .tap content inside the writable ephemeral execution workspace; those files were tracked and discarded without changing the original checkout or immutable bundle snapshot. 6. Supported and Unsupported Alpha Scope Supported Scope Runtime : Node.js 20+ Languages : Pure JavaScript or TypeScript repositories (ordinary single-package structures). Package Manager : npm with standard package-lock.json . Operating Systems : macOS and Linux hosts. Unsupported or Unverified Scope (Alpha) npm workspaces and monorepos. Yarn, pnpm, and non-npm package managers. Runtimes other than Node.js (Python, Go, etc.). Windows hosts. Reuse of native host-compiled binaries inside replay. Active network connections or remote endpoint access during replay. 7. Execution Commands and Outputs To capture, verify, and replay an execution: # Capture command execution node bin/reprospec.js capture --output my-bundle -- node -e "console.log('original run')" Output: [reprospec] Capturing: node -e console.log('original run')
[reprospec] Working directory: [reprospec] Started at: 2026-07-31T15:46:09.188Z

[reprospec] Bundle written to: /my-bundle
[reprospec] Exit code: 0
[reprospec] Status: PASS
[reprospec] Removed environment variables: ✅ Bundle written to: /my-bundle # Verify bundle integrity node bin/reprospec.js verify my-bundle Output: ── ReproSpec Bundle Verification ──────────────────────
Bundle: /my-bundle
Status: ✅ INTEGRITY_VERIFIED — The bundle manifest and SHA-256 file hashes were verified.

File Details:
  ✅ stdout.txt: OK
  ✅ stderr.txt: OK
  ✅ command.json: OK
  ✅ environment.json: OK
  ✅ integrity.json: OK
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # Replay inside Docker sandbox node bin/reprospec.js replay my-bundle Output: ── ReproSpec Replay Sandbox ───────────────────────────
Bundle: /my-bundle
Docker: v29.5.3
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

[reprospec] Running replay container: docker run --detach --name reprospec-replay- --network none --user 1000:1000 --memory 1g --cpus 1.0 --pids-limit 128 --security-opt no-new-privileges=true --read-only --env REPROSPEC_REPLAY=1 --env HOME=/tmp -v :/workspace --workdir /workspace --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m --stop-timeout 60 node:20-alpine node -e console.log('original run')

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 8. Specific Technical Feedback Request We are looking for developer feedback on: How you handle test suites requiring local databases or external configurations offline. Caching policies for npm packages to prevent native binary mismatches. Check out the repository and prerelease: Repository : https://github.com/HenryParker37-VIP/reprospec Prerelease : https://github.com/HenryParker37-VIP/reprospec/releases/tag/v0.1.0-alpha.2 9. The Maintainer Problem

When a bug report is filed, maintainers often must choose between setting up a matching VM environment or triaging based on static text logs.

The Information Gap in Ordinary Logs

Ordinary logs are useful, but they usually do not include a standardized integrity manifest, a portable environment summary, and a documented local replay workflow in one bundle.

ReproSpec is an experimental CLI and evidence-bundle format designed to bridge this gap.

1. Bundle Structure

A ReproSpec bundle contains the following schema layout (reprospec.bundle/v0.1-alpha):

  • manifest.json: Metadata, schema version, and security exceptions.
  • command.json: Captured command parameters, exit code, and duration.
  • environment.json: Node runtime details, scrubbed environment variables.
  • stdout.txt / stderr.txt: Process logs.
  • integrity.json: SHA-256 hash index of the declared files.
  • EVIDENCE_CARD.md: A human-readable markdown report card.
2. Capture & Redaction Workflow

When you run reprospec capture -- , ReproSpec:

  • Spawns the command and records its output streams.
  • Slices each of stdout and stderr streams individually to enforce a strict 10MB limit.
  • Runs a regex redaction processor to remove supported credential patterns (such as ghp_ tokens) from stdout, stderr, environment keys, and command arguments.

⚠️ Argument Immutability: ReproSpec executes the captured command with its original arguments to ensure program behavior is unchanged. Redaction is applied only to the persisted evidence representation.

3. Integrity Limitations

Verification re-calculates hashes against integrity.json.

⚠️ Important Limit: This only detects changes relative to the SHA-256 hashes recorded in the bundle manifest. A party able to rewrite the entire bundle could also recompute those hashes. It does not prove author identity or captured trace truthfulness.

4. Replay Sandbox Parity & Boundaries
  • Immutable Source Snapshot: Capture stores the required source content inside the evidence bundle under snapshot/, with relative paths, sizes, and SHA-256 hashes in snapshot.json and the bundle integrity manifest.
  • Writable Disposable Execution: Before replay, ReproSpec verifies the immutable snapshot and copies it into a new ephemeral execution workspace. Only that disposable copy is mounted writable, so ordinary build and test commands can create dist, coverage, cache, and temporary files.
  • No Original Checkout Mount: The original checkout and evidence bundle are not mounted into replay. allowWorkspaceMount is disabled and blocked in the Alpha.2 replay path.
  • Output Handling: Replay records stdout, stderr, the exit-code oracle result, and files created, modified, or deleted in the execution workspace. The workspace and generated files are removed after success, failure, or timeout; generated files are never added back to the evidence snapshot.
  • Dependency Isolation: An ephemeral build container uses npm ci with network access to fetch packages based on package-lock.json. It runs without host credentials, home-directory mounts, Docker socket access, or inherited variables.
  • Offline Replay: The actual replay container runs offline with --network none.
  • Host Check: The CLI compares git status before and after replay, failing if any host changes occur.
5. Lessons from the Three-Repository Pilot

During early testing against real repositories, we encountered several portability limits:

  1. Vercel's ms package: Replay failed because Jest 30 preset resolution (ts-jest) failed to resolve correctly relative to the isolated workspace root under Node 20.
  2. dotenv package: The exact public commit c0e32b8267b69a438bc0cc31345f73b5e2f037db passed the Node.js 20 baseline and Alpha.2 clean-room replay. Its build and test workflow generated dist and .tap content inside the writable ephemeral execution workspace; those files were tracked and discarded without changing the original checkout or immutable bundle snapshot.
6. Supported and Unsupported Alpha Scope Supported Scope
  • Runtime: Node.js 20+
  • Languages: Pure JavaScript or TypeScript repositories (ordinary single-package structures).
  • Package Manager: npm with standard package-lock.json.
  • Operating Systems: macOS and Linux hosts.
Unsupported or Unverified Scope (Alpha)
  • npm workspaces and monorepos.
  • Yarn, pnpm, and non-npm package managers.
  • Runtimes other than Node.js (Python, Go, etc.).
  • Windows hosts.
  • Reuse of native host-compiled binaries inside replay.
  • Active network connections or remote endpoint access during replay.
7. Execution Commands and Outputs

To capture, verify, and replay an execution:

title: React Mastery Series – Day 19: Routing in React – Building Single Page Applications with React Router
summary:
Welcome back to the React Mastery Series ! In the previous article, we explored Custom Hooks in React and learned how reusable logic helps developers build scalable and maintainable applications. Today, we will explore one of the most important concepts in modern frontend development: React Routing Almost every real-world React application contains multiple screens: Login Dashboard Profile Settings Reports Transactions Admin panels But React applications are usually built as: Single Page Applications (SPA) So how do we navigate between different pages without refreshing the browser? The answer is React Router What is Client-Side Routing? Traditional websites work like this: User Clicks Link
       |
       ↓
Browser Requests New HTML Page
       |
       ↓
Server Sends Page
       |
       ↓
Browser Reloads Every navigation causes a full page refresh. React Single Page Applications work differently: User Clicks Link
       |
       ↓
React Router Intercepts Request
       |
       ↓
URL Changes
       |
       ↓
React Loads Component
       |
       ↓
No Page Refresh This creates a smooth application experience. What is React Router? React Router is a library that enables navigation between different components based on the URL. Example: /login
/dashboard
/profile
/settings Each URL maps to a React component. Example: /login
   |
   ↓
Login Component


/dashboard

summary_html:
Welcome back to the React Mastery Series!

In the previous article, we explored Custom Hooks in React and learned how reusable logic helps developers build scalable and maintainable applications.

Today, we will explore one of the most important concepts in modern frontend development:

React Routing

Almost every real-world React application contains multiple screens:

  • Login
  • Dashboard
  • Profile
  • Settings
  • Reports
  • Transactions
  • Admin panels

But React applications are usually built as:

Single Page Applications (SPA)

So how do we navigate between different pages without refreshing the browser?

The answer is React Router

What is Client-Side Routing?

Traditional websites work like this:

User Clicks Link
       |
       ↓
Browser Requests New HTML Page
       |
       ↓
Server Sends Page
       |
       ↓
Browser Reloads

Every navigation causes a full page refresh.

React Single Page Applications work differently:

User Clicks Link
       |
       ↓
React Router Intercepts Request
       |
       ↓
URL Changes
       |
       ↓
React Loads Component
       |
       ↓
No Page Refresh

This creates a smooth application experience.

What is React Router?

React Router is a library that enables navigation between different components based on the URL.

Example:

/login
/dashboard
/profile
/settings

Each URL maps to a React component.

Example:

/login
   |
   ↓
Login Component


/dashboard
   |
   ↓
Dashboard Component
Installing React Router

For a React application:

npm install react-router-dom

The package provides:

  • BrowserRouter
  • Routes
  • Route
  • Link
  • Navigate
  • useNavigate
  • useParams
Setting Up BrowserRouter

The first step is wrapping your application.

Example:

import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router-dom";

import App from "./App";

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <App />
  BrowserRouter>,
);

Now React can manage browser navigation.

Creating Routes

Routes define which component should display for a URL.

Example:

import { Routes, Route } from "react-router-dom";

function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />

      <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />

      <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
    Routes>
  );
}

Now:

/login

renders:

<Login />
Understanding Route Components

Example:

<Route path="/profile" element={<Profile />} />;

Contains path and element

The URL path specifies the url appeared in browser

Example:

/profile
element

The component to render on visiting the path specified.

Example:

<Profile />
Navigation Using Link

Traditional HTML - causes a browser refresh.

 href="/dashboard"> Dashboard

React Router provides:

import { Link } from "react-router-dom";
<Link to="/dashboard">DashboardLink>

Benefits:

  • No page refresh
  • SPA behavior
  • Better performance
Creating a Navigation Bar

Example:

function Navbar() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <Link to="/">HomeLink>

      <Link to="/dashboard">DashboardLink>

      <Link to="/profile">ProfileLink>
    nav>
  );
}

When users click:

Dashboard

React loads:

<Dashboard />

without refreshing.

Programmatic Navigation with useNavigate

Sometimes navigation happens after an action.

Examples:

  • Successful login
  • Logout
  • Form submission

Example:

import { useNavigate } from "react-router-dom";

function Login() {
  const navigate = useNavigate();

  function handleLogin() {
    // API success

    navigate("/dashboard");
  }

  return <button onClick={handleLogin}>Loginbutton>;
}

Flow:

User Login
     |
     ↓
API Success
     |
     ↓
navigate("/dashboard")
     |
     ↓
Dashboard Page
Route Parameters

Many applications need dynamic URLs.

Example:

/users/101

Here:

101

is dynamic.

React Router supports this using parameters.

Example:

<Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserDetails />} />
Reading Route Parameters

Using:

useParams()

Example:

import { useParams } from "react-router-dom";

function UserDetails() {
  const { id } = useParams();

  return <h2>User ID: {id}h2>;
}

URL:

/users/101

Output:

User ID: 101
Real-World Example: Banking Application

Consider:

/accounts/12345

where:

12345

is the account number.

Route:

<Route path="/accounts/:accountId" element={<AccountDetails />} />

Component:

const { accountId }=useParams();

Now the application knows which account to display.

Nested Routes

Large applications often have sections inside sections.

Example:

Dashboard

   |
   ├── Overview

   ├── Transactions

   └── Profile

Routes:

<Route>
  <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} >
  <Route path="transactions" element={<Transactions />} />
  <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
Routes>

URL:

/dashboard/transactions

renders:

Dashboard
    +
Transactions
Outlet Component

Nested routes use:

<Outlet />

Example:

import { Outlet } from "react-router-dom";

function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Dashboardh1>

      <Outlet />
    div>
  );
}

The child route appears where Outlet exists.

Protected Routes

Enterprise applications often require authentication.

Example:

Users should access:

/dashboard

only after login.

Without authentication:

/dashboard
       |
       ↓
Redirect
       |
       ↓
/login
Creating ProtectedRoute

Example:

function ProtectedRoute({ children }) {
  const isAuthenticated = true;

  if (!isAuthenticated) {
    return <Navigate to="/login" />;
  }

  return children;
}

Usage:

<Route
  path="/dashboard"

  element={
    <ProtectedRoute>
      <Dashboard />
    ProtectedRoute>
  }
/>;
Real-World Authentication Flow

Enterprise applications usually follow:

User Opens Application

        |
        ↓

Check Token

        |
        ↓

Token Exists?

        |
   -------------
   |           |
 Yes           No
   |            |
Dashboard     Login

React Router handles navigation decisions.

Lazy Loading Routes

Large applications should not load every page immediately.

Example:

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import("./Dashboard") );

Route:

<Suspense fallback="Loading...">
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
  Routes>
Suspense>;

Benefits:

  • Smaller initial bundle
  • Faster startup
  • Better performance
Route Organization in Enterprise Projects

A scalable structure:

src

├── routes
│    ├── AppRoutes.jsx
│    ├── ProtectedRoute.jsx
├── pages
│    ├── Login.jsx
│    ├── Dashboard.jsx
│    └── Profile.jsx
├── layouts
│    └── MainLayout.jsx
Real-World Banking Application Routing

Example:

/login

/dashboard

/accounts

/accounts/:id

/transactions

/profile

/settings

Flow:

Login
 |
 ↓
Authentication Success
 |
 ↓
Dashboard
 |
 ├── Accounts
 |
 ├── Transactions
 |
 └── Profile

This is the architecture used in many enterprise React applications.

Common Mistakes 1. Using Anchor Tags

Avoid:

 href="/dashboard"> Dashboard

Use:

<Link to="/dashboard"> Dashboard Link>
2. Forgetting BrowserRouter

Without:

<BrowserRouter>

routing will not work.

3. Incorrect Nested Routes

Parent route must contain:

<Outlet />

otherwise child routes won't appear.

4. Loading All Pages at Startup

Large applications should use:

  • lazy loading
  • code splitting
Best Practices
  • Keep routes centralized.
  • Use lazy loading for large applications.
  • Create reusable protected routes.
  • Use meaningful URL structures.
  • Avoid unnecessary route nesting.
  • Separate page components from reusable components.
Key Takeaways

Today, we learned:

✅ React Router enables navigation in Single Page Applications.
✅ Routes map URLs to React components.
✅ Link provides SPA navigation without refresh.
✅ useNavigate enables programmatic navigation.
✅ useParams reads dynamic route values.
✅ Protected routes secure application pages.
✅ Lazy loading improves application performance.

Coming Next 🚀

In Day 20, we will explore:

Building Production-Ready React Applications – Project Structure and Architecture

We will learn:

  • Scalable folder structure
  • Component organization
  • Feature-based architecture
  • Separation of concerns
  • API service layers
  • Error handling
  • Environment configuration
  • Enterprise React project patterns

This will connect all the concepts we learned so far into a real-world production architecture.

Happy Coding! 🚀

title: Read the cold LinkedIn outreach that led Fishwife's CEO to hire a candidate
summary: Becca Millstein said this one LinkedIn message stood out. Fishwife Becca Millstein, cofounder and CEO of Fishwife, said she doesn't typically respond to DMs. However, she recently hired a candidate after they sent an effective LinkedIn outreach. She said the candidate had a great background, strong numbers to back it up, and a concise message. If you feel like your messages are getting lost in the void, you may be onto something. Executives are often bombarded with many sales pitches and introductions every day — and that makes it difficult to stand out with a cold outreach . Becca Millstein, cofounder and CEO of the trendy tinned seafood company Fishwife, said she misses many of the messages she receives on LinkedIn. "I don't respond to DMs because I don't see them, or it's just too much," Millstein told Business Insider. Millstein, who cofounded the company in 2020, said it's become increasingly difficult for candidates to stand out by sending a direct message. Every so often, though, someone manages to break through. She said a prospective employee reached out several months ago. After seeing the message, she passed it on to the hiring manager, and they ultimately hired the candidate. An anonymized version of the DM is below: Hi Becca, I just applied for the ______ role at Fishwife and wanted to introduce myself. In ______ years at ______, I've scaled ______  from ______ to ______ M orders/year. I oversee end-to-end ______, including ______, while managing the corresponding budget of $______ M/year. In addition to leading ______, I'm responsible for our relationships and agreements with ______. I use data to forecast ______, and to optimize______. The best part of my role is the cross-functional collaboration with teams like ______. Would you be open to a conversation to discuss the role further? My résumé is attached for reference. Thanks! Millstein said the candidate's message got her attention because it was specific and direct. They explained which role they were interested in, summarized their relevant experience, and included numbers to make their case. She added that the message was concise and made it clear they were "clearly not a robot," which stands out in the flood of messages she receives. The CEO said that after checking the candidate out, she sent the résumé to the hiring manager and said, "This person seems awesome." Most of the messages she receives "don't have that kind of substance," Millstein said. The candidate also included their résumé in the message and said they had already applied for the job, which Millstein said was an important detail. "Never just send a message if there's a job application open," Millstein said. "Apply for that job. You'll get lost if you don't." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Your agent's memory is a vector store. Ask it "how many" and watch it fall over.
summary: Originally published at nlqdb.com/blog The standard agent-memory build is an afternoon of work: embed every fact worth keeping, upsert it into a vector store, and before each reply pull the top-k most similar memories back into context. And for what it's built for, it works. Ask "what did this user say about the Berlin migration" and the right snippets come back, ranked by cosine distance. Recall is solved enough that it feels like memory is solved. Then the agent has been running for a month, and you ask its memory a different kind of question: "how many users asked about pricing this month?" "Average deal size per stage?" "Top 10 topics I logged, ranked by count?" The store dutifully returns the twenty memories most similar to the question text , the LLM eyeballs them, and you get a confident, specific, wrong number. Recall is similarity. Reporting is aggregation. Nothing malfunctioned — the two questions want different machines. A vector store's primitive is nearest-neighbour search: embed the query, rank stored vectors by distance, return the top-k, optionally narrowed by a metadata filter. That is the whole contract. There is no COUNT , no GROUP BY , no JOIN , no HAVING — a similarity engine ships no query planner, and even the metadata filter only narrows candidates around the approximate search, so what comes back is still a ranking of similar items, never a computed result set. "How many" has to touch every matching row . If the agent logged 4,000 memories and top-k is 20, the context the LLM sees is structurally incapable of producing the count — and an LLM doing arithmetic over a retrieved sample is a hallucination generator, not a query engine. The failure is quiet, too: the answer arrives fluent and plausible, and nothing flags that it was computed from half a percent of the data. -- "top topics this month, ranked by count" is not a similarity query. -- It's this — and it must scan every matching row, not the top-k: SELECT topic , count ( * ) AS mentions FROM memories WHERE created_at >= date_trunc ( 'month' , now ()) GROUP BY topic ORDER BY mentions DESC LIMIT 10 ; So the split worth keeping: when the question is "find what's like this" — RAG context, related-document lookup, fuzzy recall over conversation — a vector store is exactly the right machine, and a managed one like Pinecone is genuinely good at it. When the question is "count, group, or rank what I stored" , the memory needs to be typed rows behind a real query planner. Neither machine substitutes for the other, and bolting a bigger LLM onto the first one doesn't turn it into the second. They compose cleanly: vector store as the recall layer, relational store as the analytical one. That second layer is what nlqdb is — a real Postgres the agent provisions itself over MCP and queries in plain English, with the compiled SQL shown so you can read exactly what ran. The honest caveat cuts the other way too: nlqdb ships no embedding search, so it is not your recall layer. Pick the store per question shape — the full side-by-side is at nlqdb vs Pinecone .

title: He turned a side hustle into a video game resale business that's brought in $4 million this year
summary: Caleb Ashton is the owner and founder of QuickFlips. QuickFlips Caleb Ashton founded QuickFlips, a platform to sell video games, consoles, and Pokémon cards. Ashton opened a storefront for his business in 2025. QuickFlips has paid customers over $5 million since 2019. Caleb Ashton's journey into the resale business was, like many who start out in that industry, humble. Ashton began flipping items — textbooks, action figures, golf clubs, sneakers, and more — while living with his wife in a one-bedroom apartment in 2019. He was eager to create an extra source of income while his wife attended law school. In true millennial fashion, he learned how to buy and resell items from YouTube videos. "I started with a budget of 500 bucks that I had cobbled together from birthday and Christmas money. That was my startup seed money," Ashton, 31, told Business Insider."I initially focused on really cheap items like books or things that I could get for $5 at yard sales." Caleb Ashton opened a storefront for his business, QuickFlips, in Kentucky. QuickFlips Ashton kept up the side hustle for about six months, but it turned into a full-time job after he was fired from a friend's collectible coin business. By that point, Ashton had learned that some items could lead to quick, reliable money. Specifically, physical video games. Things grew quickly. In 2024, he created QuickFlips , an online resale platform where people can sell their video game collections, consoles, and Pokémon trading cards . He also built the platform's buyback software system. On QuickFlips, users enter their item into the search bar to get an instant offer price. Once the QuickFlips team has inspected the incoming items, users ship them to the company and receive a payout within 24 hours. QuickFlips then resells the refurbished items on Amazon, eBay, and TCGPlayer to make a profit. As of 2025, they're also sold in Ashton's brick-and-mortar store. Users can find payout prices for different items through QuickFlips' search bar. QuickFlips Ashton opened the storefront last September in Lexington, Kentucky. The overall business made about $4 million in revenue in 2026 and has paid over $5 million to customers since its inception. Necessity becomes invention Ashton's decision to open a storefront came out of necessity. For a time, he operated QuickFlips from his spare bedroom. Then, his basement. "My first hire was my friend Spencer, who came to help pack stuff up and list inventory," Ashton said. "We ended up having about 10 employees in that basement." QuickFlips began purchasing dozens of video game collections each week. That meant storing the numerous collections, assessing the products, listing them for sale on sites like Amazon , and preparing them for shipping, all from the basement. At one point, there was so much inventory in the basement that Ashton struggled to find space for new hires. "It was way too tight. My neighbors hated me, so I knew I had to get an actual office space. We landed on a retail complex," Ashton said. QuickFlips now has 33 employees across its storefront and online platform. QuickFlips Now, QuickFlips has 33 employees across its online platform and retail space. Strategy-wide, Ashton said QuickFlip's approach to payouts is what differentiates it from other sellers in the marketplace. They have a simple motto: "Pay well, Sell fast." title: DoorDash is paying people to load its delivery robots. It points to a shortcoming of automation
summary: DoorDash is paying gig workers to load restaurant orders into its Dot robots. Bloomberg/Getty Images DoorDash's Dot delivery robot can't physically pick up restaurant orders on its own. The company is paying gig workers to cover the final feet between restaurants and the robots. DoorDash said that it's offering the loading gigs to meet demand during busy times. DoorDash's delivery robots need a hand. Some workers in areas where DoorDash is using its Dot delivery robot are receiving offers through the DoorDash app to load them up. While the vehicles can navigate miles to delivery destinations, it's the few feet between a restaurant's pickup counter and the curb outside where delivery workers intervene. Devena Bybee, a DoorDash gig worker in Mesa, Arizona, said that she received one such offer in early July. The company is using the robots to make deliveries in the Phoenix area. Bybee drove about two miles to a restaurant, picked up an order, and placed it in the Dot robot as it waited in the parking lot, she said. She took photos of each step to document the process, and the gig took five minutes, she said. DoorDash paid her about $5. Bybee was surprised that Doordash asked her to complete the task instead of a restaurant worker who was already on-site. "I just don't see how it's efficient," she said. On Facebook groups for DoorDash workers, some posts show screenshots of similar gig offers over the past month. "I would never do a five-dollar order, but I was really curious about this and I was super close to the restaurant," reads one July 6 post showing a robot-loading gig at a Burger King in Scottsdale, Arizona. The poster did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "Dashers are essential to our platform and will continue completing the majority of deliveries even as our autonomous technology scales," a DoorDash spokesperson said. "This limited pilot is designed to support merchants during busy periods, while creating more earning opportunities for Dashers outside of traditional deliveries," the spokesperson added. A sticking point for automation The loading gigs are the latest example of DoorDash workers stepping in when autonomous vehicles can't complete a job on their own. Some workers received offers from DoorDash to close open doors on Waymo's self-driving cars in Atlanta, Business Insider reported in February. Waymo plans to add a self-closing function to its vehicles in the future, the companies said at the time. Dot, which DoorDash unveiled in September, is roughly the size of a baby stroller and can hold up to 30 pounds of cargo. The robot can navigate both roads and sidewalks to travel between restaurants and customers' homes. Handing off orders from restaurants to robots is a challenge to the rollout of autonomous deliveries , DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said last August, shortly before the company debuted Dot. While loading an order only takes a few minutes, restaurants that receive lots of robot-delivered orders might have an incentive to outsource the task to DoorDash, said Robert Bruno, a professor of labor and employment relations at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. DoorDash's gig workers, who are independent contractors, don't receive the same employee benefits and hourly pay rate that most restaurant workers do, Bruno said. "Multiplied over the course of a year or more, there's probably a real savings," he said. Bybee, the DoorDash worker in Arizona, said that the loading gig left her more confident that humans are still needed for delivery work. "There's only so much right now that the robots can do," she said. Do you have a story idea about DoorDash? title: I sold my house in Miami and moved to rural North Florida. My cost of living and stress are down, and productivity is up.
summary: Cheryl Patella. Courtesy of Cheryl Patella Cheryl Patella transformed her life by moving from Miami to rural North Florida. Her move cut her commuting costs, improved her quality of life, and aligned her work with personal values. Embracing remote work, Patella now enjoys nature, reduced expenses, and intentional living in Florida. At 6 a.m. every morning, I gather fresh eggs, check the vegetable garden, breathe in the cool North Florida air, watch my dogs race across five acres, and walk into my home office to begin a virtual meeting with a client. Five years ago, my mornings began very differently. Before sunrise, I had already left my home in Miami and was in bumper-to-bumper traffic on Interstate 95. My commute to my job, which began as a fitness director and advanced to acting spa director and later as spa director at another facility, had stretched from 35 to 50 minutes, plus a 20-minute ferry ride. I paid about $65 a week in tolls, drove 20,000 to 22,000 miles each year, and accepted nearly two hours of commuting as simply part of building a successful career. I believed those sacrifices were the cost of doing business Our culture often presents a choice between pursuing success and living a simpler life. What I didn't recognize was that I was also paying hidden quality-of-life costs in time, attention, stress, and mental energy, which diminished both the quantity and quality of my work. They never appeared on a budget, yet they quietly influenced how I lived, worked, and thought. Ironically, after more than four decades helping clients improve their physical and emotional well-being as a medical fitness specialist, I hadn't fully recognized how much my own environment was shaping mine. Then COVID-19 created something unexpected For the first time in decades, life became quiet enough for me to step back and evaluate the life I had built. I suddenly found myself with enough distance from my normal routine to ask questions I had been too busy to consider before. I started looking for a vacation home where I could spend more time outdoors with my dogs. Then someone asked what my dream home would look like if I could live anywhere. I wrote it down, and the search quietly shifted toward finding a new place to live full-time. I kept picturing myself sitting at a desk in a wooded area, writing. The vision came to life while searching on Zillow and yielded three top choices. It was quite an experience searching for homes in the mountains Some were too far from anyone I knew, and others would have a serious winter season, which was foreign to me. I flew to each of those cities and, after inspecting several properties, I made a list of the pros and cons of each. It came down to a North Florida property. It was closer to family and a bit larger than I had in mind, but it had all the specifics I was looking for: woods, land, seasonal changes, and they accepted a lower offer. As a Christian, I've always made prayer part of my decision-making. Over time, I became convinced God wasn't asking me to escape my life — he was asking me to realign it. The decision also made practical sense Real estate in South Florida had skyrocketed, and my home in Miami had appreciated substantially. Selling it allowed me to buy 5.5 acres at 59% of my Miami home's selling price, left me with the funds needed for remodeling and upgrades, and reduced recurring expenses. I moved some of my clients to a new trainer who was a good fit for them. Two clients wished to remain with me and work remotely. The home I bought was a foreclosure, which meant it could take three months or more to close, requiring me to stay in a rental or hotel with my dogs — another serious adjustment. Finally spending almost two years remodeling the house tested my patience more than I expected. Like any worthwhile investment, the return has unfolded over time. My property has appreciated to double the price I paid for it. Nearly five years later, I can say it was worth every challenge Patella with her dogs on her porch. Courtesy of Cheryl Patella In South Florida, I spent weekends on my Jet Ski . Flying across Biscayne Bay felt like the perfect escape from a demanding workweek. Occasionally, dolphins would surface nearby, jumping alongside me as I crossed the water. I've traded my Jet Ski for a Hustler zero-turn lawn mower. I spend time maintaining pastures, tending gardens, and caring for the property that has become my sanctuary. The wildlife encounters haven't disappeared — they've simply changed. I now watch small herds of deer graze peacefully in the fields. Some of the financial benefits were obvious. My auto insurance premium dropped from $280 to about $125 a month after moving north. Homeowners insurance fell from roughly $4,000 a year to $1,800, and property taxes declined from $4,000 annually to $1,600. My monthly fuel bill was cut by more than half, tolls virtually disappeared, and my current vehicle, purchased new in 2023, has under 20,000 miles after nearly three years. My work has changed as well Technology allows me to work with clients across the country, but the biggest change wasn't where I work — it was how I work. For years, I managed teams of 30 to 40 employees while supporting communities of several thousand elite residents. It was fulfilling, but every day required constant decisions, interruptions, staffing issues, and operational problem-solving. Today, my office overlooks gardens, open fields, and woods. When I need a break, I step outside and walk the property, work in the garden, or watch deer cross the pasture before returning to my desk. Other changes happened because my environment changed Living in Miami made it easy to stop for lunch, meet friends for dinner, shop on the way home, or spend money simply because everything was convenient. I'd always encouraged my clients to prepare meals in advance because it saves time, reduces impulse eating, and lowers food costs. Living in a rural community makes it easier to consistently practice those habits. Restaurants are no longer around every corner, and shopping has become intentional rather than convenient. Weekly dry cleaning, salon appointments, dog-walking services, and a home alarm system disappeared. Professional suits and designer shoes gradually gave way to jeans, work boots, and workout clothes. Acreage, however, requires equipment, fencing, landscaping, and continual upkeep that doesn't exist on a suburban lot. Travel is less convenient, too. Instead of flying directly from Miami to almost anywhere, most trips now require connections. There are other trade-offs I miss having my niece and her children nearby, but we talk almost daily, and we've traveled together around the US and to Europe. I also miss my longtime housekeeper, who knew my home, my routines, and my dogs almost as well as I did. Every meaningful decision asks us to give something up Somewhere along the way, I became so immersed in the business of doing business that I stopped evaluating my quality of life. Living in the country doesn't equate with loneliness, as my days are still filled with Zooms and FaceTimes. I have close neighbors who watch out for me, and when I need something, I call them. The difference is that I traded constant interruption for intentional connection. My cost of living declined, my productivity increased, my stress level fell, and my quality of life has improved, but the greatest return wasn't measured by lower insurance premiums, fewer tolls, or a shorter commute. It came from finally aligning my faith, my values, my work, and the life I wanted to build. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: At an ex-OpenAI researcher's influential lab, $500,000 salaries aren't enough to fix a talent 'bottleneck'
summary: METR's CEO, Beth Barnes, and president, Chris Painter. METR METR, a Berkeley lab started by an ex-OpenAI researcher, has grown into a prominent AI umpire. The nonprofit works with OpenAI, Anthropic, and governments to evaluate cutting-edge models. METR says that an AI talent shortage hinders growth in safety and security research. Beth Barnes, one of the AI industry's most influential watchdogs, has a lot to worry about. The ex-OpenAI researcher has shown that AI's capabilities are escalating by the month . Now, she fears that the industry doesn't have the staff in place to keep up with the technology in its next chapter. The biggest barrier to that research is talent, said Barnes, who left OpenAI to start the nonprofit METR in 2022. METR, which stands for Model Evaluation and Threat Research, plays a crucial role in the AI industry by working closely with OpenAI, Anthropic , Google, and Meta to provide independent answers about the tech's quickly changing capabilities. Yet Barnes sees such fierce competition for AI researchers that even METR's lofty salaries, which reach $503,000 on current job postings, don't address the nonprofit's talent shortage. "Ideally, we'd like to scale really large, but in practice, we've been able to fundraise as much as we need, and the bottleneck is much more talent," Barnes said. The security incident announced by OpenAI and Hugging Face sparked a new wave of questions about how to evaluate and control AI. More than 1,300 frontier lab employees signed a letter in July warning that AI development could outpace control. title: Reviews are ruining your life
summary: Getty Images; iStock; Tyler Le/BI James Hardaway has a reputation among his friends and family for being a reviews guy . Before making a big purchase, he'll check Wirecutter and Consumer Reports, do a drive-by of Reddit , and see what's being said on YouTube. He's an avid film fan, and he eagerly combs through Rotten Tomatoes scores and media writeups ahead of new releases to make sure he's in tune with the cultural moment. He feels that if he's not doing his homework, he may not be making the best use of his money. Still, Hardaway, a 38-year-old manufacturing manager in Texas, isn't sure if all the ratings-related rigamarole is meaningfully improving his life. He and his wife spent $450 on the supposed "best" stroller when their first child was born and swapped it out for cheaper options in a matter of months. He's not in love with their reviews-driven dishwasher or mattress, though he does like the internet-approved noise machine. For the most part, all the choices and all the noise leave him constantly wondering whether he could have done better. "There are more and more things that are getting reviewed," he says. "Maybe I don't need the best plunger, but something in my brain thinks that I do." Many Americans treat every product, service, and experience they buy like a research project. In 2016, the Pew Research Center found that eight in 10 Americans read online reviews before buying something for the first time, and more recent industry surveys suggest the habit has only become more entrenched. Case in point: a 2026 Yelp questionnaire found that an overwhelming majority of Gen Z consumers do research on at least one platform before picking a restaurant, gym, or beauty salon. Reviews are a remarkably useful invention that let us tap into the wisdom of the crowd. However, we may be taking review culture too far. We're drowning in endless options and endless opinions about those options. It leaves us less satisfied with our selections and strips spontaneity even from simple picks. Instead of helping us make good decisions quickly, reviews tempt us to believe there's some perfect decision to be found if we just keep scrolling. "Once you're out for the best, the path to misery is pretty straight," says Barry Schwartz, a professor emeritus in social theory and social action at Swarthmore College and the author of the book " The Paradox of Choice ." "It's the price we pay for getting what we said we wanted — which we shouldn't have wanted — which is unlimited options." Reviews have democratized information. Instead of relying on brand marketing or a newspaper critic (a dying breed anyway), people can learn from the experience of hundreds of other customers. But the volume of it all makes it easy to get overwhelmed. It's a familiar experience: You decide to have, say, pizza for dinner and start browsing through the local options. After 30 minutes, you've identified 15 possible restaurants and read dozens of reviews, and you are still no closer to a decision. One pizza is probably better than the other, but also, any pizza is probably fine, and here you are spending most of your Tuesday night on an unexpected, illogical quest to identify the ideal pie. Once you're out for the best, the path to misery is pretty straight. "One can get overly indexed on trying to find the best of something or all the information that they could find to make that perfect decision about it," says Michael Luca, a professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. "When do we need to be optimizing? When do we need to be satisficing? And just finding something that works for what we're looking to do?" The internet reinforces the instinct. Google surfaces stars before websites, Amazon displays reviews before a price, and AI search engines increasingly summarize the online consensus before users see a link. Small businesses live and die by the algorithms and online rating systems. Having such an abundance of options can lead to anxiety and decision paralysis . Take the earlier dinner example: You may feel so inundated or dispirited that you forgo the pizza entirely and head to the kitchen to make a sandwich. Moreover, tastes vary, and we often don't know much, if anything, about the people whose perspectives we're using for guidance. "You're flipping coins because you don't know the source of any of these reviews, but somehow it gives your decision a certain authority that otherwise it wouldn't have," Schwartz says. The fact that our consumer choices are so intertwined with our identities gives each decision more weight, he adds: "The stakes go up for even trivial decisions, and that pushes even more in the direction of looking at what other people have to say and letting that guide your own decisions." As though the reviews themselves weren't enough, artificial intelligence is increasingly deciding which reviews people see and how they're interpreted, adding in a layer of complication for consumers and businesses alike. Some platforms are using AI to summarize reviews, boiling down hundreds of opinions into a handful of sentences. This may help consumers get a general sense of the feedback and make the reviews section feel more useful, but it also has its drawbacks. Power users who like to comb through ratings aren't going to get a lot out of a summary, and while research shows that AI summaries increase purchase intention for products like electronics and appliances, they don't move the needle for experiences, like restaurants and hotels. It's also not always clear whether an AI overview is accurate or surfaces the most pertinent information. It can flatten commentary into a generic package, overrepresent a small number of negative comments in an effort to be "fair," or simply get things wrong. On sites such as Reddit, it's easy to find small business owners lamenting that AI summaries include extra-negative or incorrect content. "AI could be helpful if it's helping to figure out how to tailor information and combine it to one's own preferences. But if it's doing more of a one-size-fits-all summary, it's not clear that it's getting you closer to that thing that specifically fits your preferences," Luca says. Doug Straton, the chief marketing officer at Bazaarvoice, a software company that helps brands collect and display ratings and reviews, says that when AI platforms crawl the web for reviews, they tend to look at volume, recency, and average rating. That is used to determine which products the bot talks about, but not necessarily what it says or the context opinions are coming from — maybe the reviewer the AI is channeling never likes the scent of cucumber, so they rate a bodywash negatively because of that, and all the AI reader sees is that it smells bad. "Because you're superficially scraping the sites, you don't have this depth of data," he says. Straton's company is working with AI companies to place more weight on the Bazaarvoice community's reviews, which they say are more trustworthy and thorough than the random ones. AI, of course, brings with it another issue: fakery . It's easier than ever to use AI tools to spin up reviews, and harder than ever for consumers to know what's AI-generated. To be sure, fake reviews are hardly new — Kay Dean, a former federal criminal investigator and the founder of Fake Review Watch, an industry watchdog, tells me they've long been a "massive" problem and that platforms aren't aggressive enough in cracking down on it. "They sweep it under the carpet," she says. You make a lot of choices, and most of them are irrelevant and unmemorable. There are all sorts of tactics, AI-related and otherwise, for engaging in review-related trickery, Dean says. Some businesses will barter and trade reviews, or even go to Facebook groups to enlist reviewers, while marketers may enlist review brokers. "There's a whole cottage industry of review providers," she says. "There is a robust black market, openly and flagrantly." The Federal Trade Commission has tried to crack down on fake reviews and, in 2024, put in place a rule that bans false ratings and testimonials, prohibits incentivizing reviews with a specific sentiment, and imposes financial penalties on violators. "It was a good step, but the review platforms escape liability," Dean says, because under federal law, online companies generally aren't liable for the content other people post on their platforms. We don't need to go back to a reviews-free society, where your best hope is that your neighbor has a decent recommendation for a contractor, but we probably could stand to adjust our approach when every single thing we might try or buy comes with a giant ratings system. Sheena Iyengar, a professor at Columbia Business School who studies choice and innovation, says it really helps for people to have clarity on their preferences and goals before diving into the online comments. If you're just looking for the "best" bar or the "best" gym, you're going to have a lot of work ahead of you and may very well end up disappointed. If, however, you're looking for a decent espresso martini at a relatively quiet place with lots of seating or an establishment with plenty of weights and spin classes, you're likely to be more satisfied with the results. We often flip through reviews faster than our brains can process the information, and in those cases, it's important to slow down, especially when it's a big decision, like booking a vacation . It's also key to remember that in the vast majority of situations, it's just not that deep. "You make a lot of choices, and most of them are irrelevant and unmemorable," Iyengar says. "Most of your choices in life, because of information overload, you probably should make them on autopilot, save your cognitive energy for the choices that matter." That's easier said than done for all the aforementioned reasons — the drive to find the best, the sense that every purchase says something about our identity. Yet there's something to be said for going with the flow. If the point of an evening is to catch up with a friend, there's no need to walk 20 blocks to what Yelp and TikTok say is the most happening spot instead of stopping at one of the eight places you pass on the way. Plus, you might discover at the end of your walk that a bunch of other optimization-seekers had the same idea, and now the place is too crowded to get in. Hardaway still checks reviews and probably always will. But he's learned the online chatter isn't the gospel and that no matter how much research he does, things may not work out. Sometimes, the best baby stroller isn't the one the gurus recommend — it's the one you actually wind up using. title: Third places are out, as prices rise. Hosting dinners, craft nights, and book clubs are in.
summary: Emily O'Brien and her friends have been meeting up for book club every month for roughly a year. Rachel Wisniewski for BI Emily O'Brien, 26, said in mid-July that she had about 200 pages to go in "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez, before attending book club at a friend's place the following week. She loves attending the monthly meet-up, which friends take turns hosting at their homes in Philadelphia, a tradition they started roughly a year ago. She finished what she needed to read before gathering with her friends on a rooftop. Talking about the book is less important than making sure the friends meet every month to catch up without breaking the bank, she said. title: Top economist Steve Hanke told us why he doubts AI will be the job destroyer many expect
summary: Steve Hanke says AI costs too much to be a major threat to jobs. Steve Hanke Steve Hanke says AI won't be the game changer many people imagine as it's "incredibly costly." The leading economist said the water, power, and microchips needed to power AI limit its potential. Hanke said that many companies won't replace people with AI because human labor will be cheaper. The idea that artificial intelligence will be free to use and virtually costless to provide is delusional and dumb, Steve Hanke says . "This belief is based on a disconnect from reality, as well as a good dose of idiotic economic reasoning," the professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University told Business Insider by email. "AI is incredibly costly; it is very resource intensive," Hanke continued. "It requires huge amounts of water, power, and physical capital" like graphics chips, he added. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta have projected roughly $700 billion in combined capital expenditures this year, and $1 trillion in 2027, as they race to build out the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI models. Hanke, who served on President Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, also addressed widespread concerns that AI will cause massive job destruction . "Businesses will not be firing everybody and replacing them with AI ," he said, because in many cases that will be a lot more expensive than employing humans. The veteran economist took aim at AI visionaries, describing many of them as "charlatans and hucksters." He said they're "comparing apples and oranges" when they liken AI to software, as providing AI to customers costs money whereas software, once developed, can be sold countless times at virtually no additional cost. Hanke predicted the "cost of scarce resources that are gobbled up by AI will decide how far the 'AI revolution' goes." AI optimists have countered that technological advances will make microchips and data centers more power-efficient over time, bringing down the cost of AI. Elon Musk has made waves for predicting that AI will supercharge productivity and drive down production costs, ushering in an era of abundance where "anyone can have whatever stuff they want." The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has recommended people stop saving for retirement in 10 or 20 years as "money won't matter." Personal finance and AI experts previously told Business Insider they resoundingly disagreed with Musk's advice. Musk has predicted AI will take over most jobs, and the "best way" for governments to deal with the resulting unemployment is to provide a "universal high income" by mailing checks to everyone. Mounting concerns about AI Hanke has been skeptical of AI for a while, describing it to Business Insider in February as "overhyped and potentially dangerous." Last fall , Hanke said the AI boom could falter if Big Tech companies failed to hit their numbers, and said it "might be wise to buckle your seat belt." Mark Cuban, the former "Shark Tank" investor, and Michael Burry of "The Big Short" fame warned this week about the massive scale of AI spending and Nvidia's key role in financing it, underlining Hanke's concern about how much the technology costs. Cuban said it was "truly scary" how central Nvidia is to the AI boom, and cautioned it "all could crumble" if the chipmaker gets outcompeted or makes a mistake. Burry said Nvidia was "overreaching" in its campaign to strike deals with customers to support its chip sales, and its efforts threatened to "push the circular spending to biblical proportions." title: NVIDIA AI Releases Molt: A PyTorch-Native Agentic Reinforcement Learning Framework
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning research is constant algorithm modification. New estimators, new pipeline stages, new rollout schemes. In mainstream frameworks each change threads through layers of trainer, distributed backend, and rollout glue. That cost lands on the researcher at every iteration. Molt , from NVIDIA’s NeMo team, targets that cost directly. Its a PyTorch-native agentic RL framework with an unusual design target. The codebase should be compact enough for a researcher to hold in their head, and for an AI coding assistant to read and reason about in its entirety. The stated footprint is roughly 8.6K lines of RL code, measured by tracing the import graph from each framework’s RL entry point. The same method counts about 62K lines for verl, 25K for slime, and 7.2K for OpenRLHF. Is it deployable? Yes. Molt ships under Apache 2.0 with launch codes, Slurm scripts, and a prebuilt container. But the research paper positions it as research infrastructure, not a production training service, and hardware is the real gate. The shipped recipes assume 2 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs, split 8 for training and 8 for rollout. That puts Molt in reach of frontier and frontier-adjacent labs, well-funded AI startups doing post-training, enterprise AI research groups in finance, healthcare, and robotics that train agents against proprietary environments, and academic labs with multi-node H100/H200 access. Applications include multi-turn tool-use agents, code-execution agents, vision-language environments (the shipped geo3k recipe), LLM-as-judge reward loops, and on-policy distillation onto a smaller student. Three components, one loop Molt composes Ray for placement and asynchronous queues, vLLM for rollout, and NVIDIA AutoModel with FSDP2 for training. None of the three is forked, so upstream improvements arrive as a container pin rather than a rebase. The runtime is an agent pool, a set of vLLM engines behind a request router, and a single trainable policy actor. A streaming pool keeps prompt groups in flight so engines never drain while the actor trains. Partial rollout pauses the engines, broadcasts actor shards over NCCL directly to each engine, and resumes retained requests instead of discarding them. The agent is an ordinary program An RL run names one Python module that exports an AgentRunner . Everything else is ordinary code, including the reward. Two forms are supported. With Env , the framework owns the LLM loop in a Gymnasium-aligned step() . With ChatAgent , the user owns the loop through a stock OpenAI or Anthropic SDK. Molt launches a loopback server that speaks both wire protocols, and every request decodes server-side into one token-exact accumulation. When a long-horizon agent compacts its context and rewrites the prefix, the server seals the current segment and opens a fresh one automatically. Never train on a token you did not generate Three correctness invariants organize the design. Token identity: sampled token ids define the trajectory, not a retokenized transcript. Policy-version semantics: trainable tokens keep their behavior-policy log-probabilities, and asynchronous use is corrected per token behind a sequence-level gate. Forward consistency: rollout and actor must agree on model semantics. For mixture-of-experts policies, the last invariant matters most. The rollout and training routers select experts independently, and small numerical differences can flip top-k choices. Molt applies rollout routing replay , where vLLM returns its per-token expert ids and the training forward replays them. Interactive explainer Key Takeaways Molt is an Apache-2.0 agentic RL framework in about 8.6K lines of RL code, roughly 7× smaller than verl. Ray, vLLM, and NVIDIA AutoModel are composed, never forked, so upstream releases arrive as a container pin. Agents are plain Python; a stock OpenAI or Anthropic SDK trains as-is through a token-exact loopback server. Throughput is statistically comparable to a Megatron-based stack, with the MoE-mismatch caveat disclosed. Scale is a flag: the same loop runs a dense 4B model and a 700B MoE at --fsdp.ep_size 256 . summary_html:
Agentic reinforcement learning research is constant algorithm modification. New estimators, new pipeline stages, new rollout schemes. In mainstream frameworks each change threads through layers of trainer, distributed backend, and rollout glue. That cost lands on the researcher at every iteration.

Molt, from NVIDIA’s NeMo team, targets that cost directly. Its a PyTorch-native agentic RL framework with an unusual design target. The codebase should be compact enough for a researcher to hold in their head, and for an AI coding assistant to read and reason about in its entirety. The stated footprint is roughly 8.6K lines of RL code, measured by tracing the import graph from each framework’s RL entry point. The same method counts about 62K lines for verl, 25K for slime, and 7.2K for OpenRLHF.

Is it deployable?

Yes. Molt ships under Apache 2.0 with launch codes, Slurm scripts, and a prebuilt container. But the research paper positions it as research infrastructure, not a production training service, and hardware is the real gate. The shipped recipes assume 2 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs, split 8 for training and 8 for rollout.

That puts Molt in reach of frontier and frontier-adjacent labs, well-funded AI startups doing post-training, enterprise AI research groups in finance, healthcare, and robotics that train agents against proprietary environments, and academic labs with multi-node H100/H200 access. Applications include multi-turn tool-use agents, code-execution agents, vision-language environments (the shipped geo3k recipe), LLM-as-judge reward loops, and on-policy distillation onto a smaller student.

Three components, one loop

Molt composes Ray for placement and asynchronous queues, vLLM for rollout, and NVIDIA AutoModel with FSDP2 for training. None of the three is forked, so upstream improvements arrive as a container pin rather than a rebase.

The runtime is an agent pool, a set of vLLM engines behind a request router, and a single trainable policy actor. A streaming pool keeps prompt groups in flight so engines never drain while the actor trains. Partial rollout pauses the engines, broadcasts actor shards over NCCL directly to each engine, and resumes retained requests instead of discarding them.

The agent is an ordinary program

An RL run names one Python module that exports an AgentRunner. Everything else is ordinary code, including the reward.

Two forms are supported. With Env, the framework owns the LLM loop in a Gymnasium-aligned step(). With ChatAgent, the user owns the loop through a stock OpenAI or Anthropic SDK. Molt launches a loopback server that speaks both wire protocols, and every request decodes server-side into one token-exact accumulation. When a long-horizon agent compacts its context and rewrites the prefix, the server seals the current segment and opens a fresh one automatically.

Never train on a token you did not generate

Three correctness invariants organize the design. Token identity: sampled token ids define the trajectory, not a retokenized transcript. Policy-version semantics: trainable tokens keep their behavior-policy log-probabilities, and asynchronous use is corrected per token behind a sequence-level gate. Forward consistency: rollout and actor must agree on model semantics.

For mixture-of-experts policies, the last invariant matters most. The rollout and training routers select experts independently, and small numerical differences can flip top-k choices. Molt applies rollout routing replay, where vLLM returns its per-token expert ids and the training forward replays them.

Interactive explainer

Key Takeaways
  • Molt is an Apache-2.0 agentic RL framework in about 8.6K lines of RL code, roughly 7× smaller than verl.
  • Ray, vLLM, and NVIDIA AutoModel are composed, never forked, so upstream releases arrive as a container pin.
  • Agents are plain Python; a stock OpenAI or Anthropic SDK trains as-is through a token-exact loopback server.
  • Throughput is statistically comparable to a Megatron-based stack, with the MoE-mismatch caveat disclosed.
  • Scale is a flag: the same loop runs a dense 4B model and a 700B MoE at --fsdp.ep_size 256.
